いま なに を して います か — What are you doing now?
You say what you’re doing right now (～ています), describe states (I live, I’m married, I know) and say what’s allowed and what isn’t (～ても いい / ～ては いけません).
I live (→ すんで います)
I get married (→ けっこん して います = I’m married)
I find out (→ しって います = I know)
I hold, I have (→ もって います = I have, I own)
I work for (→ つとめて います)
(rain) falls (→ あめ が ふって います)
I wait (→ まって います)
I smoke (たばこ を) (→ すって)
I sit down (→ すわって)
I stand up, I stand (→ たって)
I put, I leave (something) (→ おいて)
To say what you’re doing right now: ～て います (I’m reading, I’m waiting, it’s raining).
To describe lasting states: すんで います, けっこん して います, しって います.
To ask permission: ～ても いい です か, and answer.
To say what’s forbidden: ～ては いけません.
To use もう (already) and まだ (not yet).
A phone call in the rain
It’s Saturday and it’s raining. Ana calls Yuki to find out where everyone is, because they want to go to a museum together.
Hello, Yuki? What are you doing now?
I’m reading a book at home right now. Because it’s raining outside.
That’s true. And Mihai? Do you know where he is?
Mihai is working at the hospital right now. He’s on duty today.
Kenji is cooking lunch at the restaurant. He’s very busy.
Then let’s go, just the two of us. I’ll wait for you in front of the museum.
Er… I don’t know the museum’s address.
No problem. I’ll send it to you by email. You have my phone number too, don’t you?
Yes, I have it. …Ah, the email’s arrived. Thanks.
(At the museum) Excuse me, may I take photos?
Ah, Yuki, no! You’re not allowed to take photos here.
Oh, really? Then may I sit here?
Yes, you may sit down. …Yuki, are you tired already?
No, not yet. I want to take my time looking at this painting.
at, in (the place of an action)
In fast speech, Japanese people swallow the i: よんで います sounds like “yonde-mas”, sometimes even “yonderu”. Say it clearly yourself, but recognise it quickly.
Watch the っ pause: shit-te. Without the pause (して) it means “doing”, something completely different!
Two pauses and a long ん: kek-ko-n. Four beats: ke-k-ko-n.
1. ～て います: an action in progress
You learned the ～て form in chapter 9. Add います and you get “I’m doing it right now” (like English “-ing” or Spanish “estoy + gerund”):
Like Spanish again! “Estoy leyendo” = よんで います. For you, learning both languages, it’s a good bridge.
Past: ～て いました (I was doing). Negative: ～て いません (I’m not doing it now).
2. ～て います: a lasting state
Some verbs describe a change that happened once and lasts. With ～て います they show the resulting state:
けっこん します (to get married)
つとめます (to join a company)
Trap: “I know” = しって います, but “I don’t know” = しりません (NOT “しって いません”). It’s a very common exception!
A typical mistake: “マドリード に すみます” for “I live in Madrid”. Correct: すんで います. すみます on its own means “I’m going to move there”.
3. May I? ～ても いい です か
The ～て form + も いい です = “it’s OK to…”. With か it becomes a question.
I’m sorry, it’s a bit… (a polite refusal)
Japanese people rarely say “no” directly. A hesitant “ちょっと…” actually means “no”.
4. Not allowed: ～ては いけません
The ～て form + は いけません = “you mustn’t…”. It’s quite strong: a teacher, a parent or a sign says it.
Between friends, more briefly: だめ です! (Not allowed! / No!).
The は in ～ては is read “wa”: “totte wa ikemasen”.
5. もう (already) and まだ (not yet)
もう ひるごはん を たべました か。 (Have you had lunch already?)
For “not yet”, Japanese people simply say まだ です. If you say “たべませんでした”, it means “I didn’t eat (and that’s that, the moment has passed)”, which sounds odd.
まだ + ～て います = “still doing”: まだ あめ が ふって います (It’s still raining).

クラブ の メンバー — The club members
Yuki wrote a short introduction to the club members for the university website.
Mihai came from Romania. He works at a hospital in Madrid.
Now he lives in a flat near the park. He’s single.
Ana teaches Spanish at a university in Spain.
Ana knows lots of Japanese songs.
Kenji has a restaurant. His wife lives in Hiroshima.
Mrs Suzuki works at the library. She has lived in Spain for fifty years.
マドリード に ゆき が ふって います — It’s snowing in Madrid
It’s a January morning. Mihai is standing at the window.
Outside, everything is white. It’s snowing!
It doesn’t snow much in Madrid. About once every ten years.
Some children are playing in the park.
There’s also a child making a snowman with his father.
A dog is running through the snow. It looks very happy.
The phone rang. It’s the hospital.
“Dr Mihai, the buses and the metro have both stopped. Can you come to the hospital?”
“Yes, I’ll walk. Because it’s only about twenty minutes.”
Mihai put on a thick coat, put on a hat and set off.
There are hardly any cars on the street. It’s very quiet.
He remembered the winters in Romania. When he was a child, he played in the snow every year.
In front of the hospital, an old lady had fallen over.
Mihai ran to her. “Are you all right?”
“My leg hurts…” It was Mrs Suzuki!
“Mrs Suzuki! Please don’t move. I’m a doctor.”
Mihai took Mrs Suzuki inside the hospital.
They X-rayed it. The bone wasn’t broken.
“Thank goodness! It’s a little swollen, but it will heal in a week.”
“Thank you, Doctor. You’re a truly kind person.”
In the afternoon a message came from Yuki.
“Mihai, what are you doing now? We’re having a snowball fight in the park!”
There was a photo too. Ana and Carlos, covered in snow, are laughing.
Mihai replied: “I’m working at the hospital right now. But I rescued Tama’s owner.”
In the evening, Mihai went home. The snow had already stopped.
In front of the building there was a little snowman.
On the snowman’s head sat a white kitten.
And in front of the snowman there was a sheet of paper.
“For Dr Mihai. Thank you for today. From everyone at the club”
Mihai smiled. It was a cold night, but his heart was warm.
The kitten jumped down from the snowman and sat at Mihai’s feet.
“Are you cold too? Then let’s go in together.”

Text to read: The inn rules
Kenji sends Mihai the rules of a traditional inn in Kyoto, for the summer trip.
Before entering the room, take off your shoes. You mustn’t go in with your shoes on.
You may wear a yukata. You may also go to the dining room in a yukata.
Before getting into the shared bath, wash your body.
You mustn’t put your towel into the hot water in the bath.
The bath may not be used from eleven at night until six in the morning.
